item.title: Clovis People Didn't Just Hunt Mammoths — They Painted and Sewed in Tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/

item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is just an instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington State to Virginia. This combination of "narrow in time, broad in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, spear points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
"Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But discoveries at sites like Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it heatedly. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the nature of the whole site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping everyone repair the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't have: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site, but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking discovery is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by an activity-dense zone, then an open area for walking further out, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact transport. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an interior space. In the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter ochre (hematite) pigment scatter was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught with traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America coexist with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), but also horse and camel. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points were found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less easily and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age — how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the "overkill" hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have upset the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single example of ancestral remains attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey doesn't find this surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the premise of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks If They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and medicines under the same regulator, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was implanted by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and medicines under the same regulator, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was implanted by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the second half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, and the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition
The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a vast, sparsely populated land leading to self-medication, pharmacists also doing diagnosis and dispensing, naturopathic industry organizations existing as early as the 1920s, and health food stores similar to food-as-medicine shops. Stacked together, these four made Australians accustomed to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic, and only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognize — for example, turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardized fish oil capsules.

12:05 The contract manufacturer is the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing for supplements, and by around 2003 it was responsible for about 70% of Australia's vitamin, mineral and herbal product production. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the rubber-and-oil seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s-90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended services in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labeling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only needs to give a concept, and the factory can turn it into a marketable product.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before market
Australia legislated in 1989, putting medicines and supplements under the TGA, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements enter the AUSTL category: they can only use low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, can only make low-level health efficacy claims, and companies can get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had about ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% belonged to this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but is actually loose
Putting the contract manufacturing and regulatory lines together: GMP only ensures the contract manufacturer produces stably according to the standards the brand gives, and that problems can be traced to batch recalls — it itself is not responsible for product efficacy. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers, and efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the saying "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is itself not wrong, but it is misleading: the regulatory method is the same, but the regulatory standard for the efficacy part differs enormously. The entire system does no effective upfront supervision of the product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and product efficacy.

25:08 The marketing learned from Centrum, not invented
CEO Radek Sali, who took office in 2008, did not come up with a marketing plan out of thin air. In his industry research he found that the best-selling peer was Centrum, and feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give terminals high profits, but it was unstoppable because it ran ads frantically on TV all year, had good athlete endorsements, and consumers would ask for it by name when entering pharmacies. Sali wanted to replicate this at Swisse. He first invested in Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's cricket team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even with a limited budget he could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel was not impressed; some buyers didn't watch cricket themselves and didn't know that athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said she liked a dance variety show, and the strategy shifted to entertainment content mentions.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger round of publicity leveraged Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with actress Nicole Kidman, pushing its reach from Australia to the US. By 2012, Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, annual revenue reached 183 million Australian dollars, and marketing spend was 40-50 million Australian dollars a year — said to have been at one point the highest marketing spend among Australian consumer brands. Its ads did not emphasize efficacy and ingredients, but mainly presented a state of being energetic, positively self-disciplined, and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse gained more than 20% market share in Australian supermarket channels and more than 10% in pharmacy channels.

32:14 The growth point was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse spent a lot of money on the US market without much success, and after returning to Australia found that Swisse sold very well in pharmacies in Chinese-concentrated areas — some stores sold ten times as much as ordinary stores — because international students and Chinese immigrants bought in bulk to take back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. In 2015 two policy shifts appeared: in March the Hangzhou Cross-Border E-Commerce Comprehensive Pilot Zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which officially took effect in December that year. The FTA mainly affected general trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average rate of 20%, and after the agreement it was said at the time that it could drop to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated as personal use in policy, so they don't need to go through the supplement import registration and filing process.

35:16 The brand was bought, the impression stayed
In September 2015, Hong Kong-listed Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full acquisition, with a deal size of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion RMB. For Swisse the deal had little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows are theoretically paid for by a Chinese supplement company, but the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their past vague good impression of Australia to it — the core value of the acquisition, to a large extent, settles in the brand goodwill part.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the ownership of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, but staged by Lenin with Stalin performing on it. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a bad orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public, was not well known in Russia, and hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia against the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had once wanted Stalin dead.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system all down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this is a complete misunderstanding of Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. It is said his intention was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won decisively. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Stalin threatened to resign whenever he was unhappy
Giles recounts a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, such as not getting authorisation at Tsaritsyn to liquidate Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew weary of it, and said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. This picture leaves the reader with something to remember: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody at the time thought the General Secretary's post worth having
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means the highest power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with him as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was furious, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really did offend her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin was moving against Lenin as he rose. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining his fluids and removing his organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode is medium density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the back half are worth more than the motivational talk in the front half.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta's data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for a single waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, exploring your own ideas and getting input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly redesigns and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made the thing changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 Designing the team matters as much as designing the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product. From that Dave derives his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences, and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — when he was 7, his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk and he felt for the first time that he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DMs to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this will become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not luck
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter spent ten years doing hardcore PDF engineering, with an understanding of Mac OS details down to the engineering level that exceeds most people's. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were ones they published. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National Park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development: buying land and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning boards.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the level of climbing Denali, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in the natural world. Dave's inference: you have to love it to that degree to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it — you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; four-plus years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimizing output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture and do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through every way someone could elicit medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks people use to get around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers are notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards made by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says flatly that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organizations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — there are no customers, nobody asking "what do you want," which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He offers counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era when electric lights spread, houses caught fire, and insurers had to pay, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards must come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 The policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building AI" and "the people buying AI." Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite amounts to saying "there is risk here, but it's manageable," and its interests align with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the loss, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet." The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as a third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright cover is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so the very act of wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance signals that you may be a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are precisely the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: with open models you don't know what they were trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits it's a hard problem and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that not unpacking open-model training data line by line is now considered broadly acceptable, so he won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals face a new challenge: agents are starting to realize they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since it means looking at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open a prediction market on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, while the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for instance, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about," and that question has no answer anywhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company cooked its books — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if we don't give you AAA, you'll go to S&P" to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the claims directly, and driving the price down just means losing their own money. He also concedes there's no perfect system: Moody's needs scrutiny, and watchdogs need scrutiny too. Asked whether the business changes if, eighteen months from now, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the issue isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons — and behaved neither like normal mice nor like cortex-less mice, but like a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," getting neither connections nor room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells are unable to divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "no-pallium mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into no-pallium pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells and already differentiated, on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, mostly replaced after removal by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They resemble neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, no-pallium mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice carrying organoids. No-pallium mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Follow-up experiments backed this up: no-pallium animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and that human cells very likely contributed some of it — but this is not perfect restoration, only evidence that these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe for humans and can bring lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to hypoxic conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and no-pallium mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a powerful system not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer, and she thinks one highlight of this work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also points out there is a long way to go: the cortex's layer structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach something more like a human brain; and the authors themselves note that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain inside a mouse brain
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing, and the cell types present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from a human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she considers this an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers who spoke to Nature share that view: these are not fully formed functional human cortices.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper, and about the work of Sergio Pasca's lab, is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as a hindrance to scientists, and that this is a genuine mistake: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so that they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a novel kind of harm that you would not easily notice, which must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents" — think of them as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, and then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper, and even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Is Not a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine, and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a firsthand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to norms — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers every week claimed ‘AI is as good as radiologists’ or ‘AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection’, but these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down sharply — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small set, the best models only matched radiologists. This is not bad news; it means there is too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially a checklist specifying which items must be reported in a paper. They don't tell you how to do the research — they are not methodological guidelines, they are transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors, and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs, no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that is hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines are produced by Delphi voting; items without consensus are cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI were not written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a set of candidate items proposed through literature review and expert opinion, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project well takes at least six months; she tried a compressed three-month version, but participants contribute their time for free, and to get high-quality feedback and multiple rounds of participation, you can't skimp on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines was fought over at the meeting
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was: should clinical trials include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said ‘No, it shouldn't be done at all, for the following reasons’. That debate was later commissioned as a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. Xiao Liu also clearly sides with ‘no’ in the lightning round: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI explainability, and keep asking until you reach the bottom — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Being a regulatory consultant without ever working in industry felt insincere to her
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the regulated side, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there, she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term, computer scientists set the direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first asked what ‘driven’ means, and after confirming it means ‘changed’, gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is — the people who process the data, choose the metrics, and choose the benchmarks determine in the short term which direction progress goes; but if the endpoint is real use in patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond, and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models continue advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the focus shifts to being ‘a companion to experience’ — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, daily wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continually need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: the ability to call on knowledge without necessarily carrying it oneself, but translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we dare not
Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her own PhD research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a bunch of diseases are loosely called ‘white dot syndromes’ just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are very likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence emerges is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious, may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, and during a period of new technological change may rigidly stick to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, missing the chance for discovery.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Condemned by His Peers for Forty Years
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.

Medium information density: the first half is medical history background, the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was ultimately diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available at the time, and it had not worked, which drove him to comb through the records of roughly 90 cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital over the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor vanished on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case of small round cell sarcoma of the neck in a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: four recurrences, and by the fifth surgery the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After the operation the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by discharge the tumor had completely disappeared. The hospital had no follow-up records, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him; in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the surgery.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could only swallow small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to laboratory-cultured bacteria, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October an injection of a culture a colleague had brought from Robert Koch's laboratory in Germany made the patient gravely ill — yet two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared, the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins rather than use live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real but only in some patients
Coley wrote in his papers that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very small number of cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly of the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he recommended it for all inoperable sarcomas (except melanotic), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, as prophylaxis after wound healing following surgery for primary sarcoma, and after surgery for all carcinomas to reduce recurrence using the mixed toxins.

19:40 JAMA watched first, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts produced complete results. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying "there is no longer much question that toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," and that although many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, not a single fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, pointing out that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and saying that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not affect the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treated roughly 1,000 cancer patients, and published about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company had been producing various preparations since 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refused to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; he insisted all cancers had a microbial origin even after that idea had been overturned; the toxins were difficult to produce and standardize; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation stole his window of time
Coley's own methods were also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different durations. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost by feel rather than by data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, and admitted that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard therapy for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry, slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for her father
After Coley died, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, but ended up delving deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully went through all her father's publications, trying to find out why some cases succeeded and others failed. In 1953, with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr., she founded the Cancer Research Institute, with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. The Cancer Research Institute today has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about her shifting UBI stance is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries send you a pre-filled return and you only fix the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it is an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it is different in kind: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of the beneficiary.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: fraud exploded after deregulation in 2020, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects this outright: the fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, and from the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs and concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who do not commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: the fraud narrative is often used to make programs look illegitimate, and thereby get voters to tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (cooking while on hold is recorded as one activity), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with staff and accountants, with one exception: to renovate a house in San Francisco, no amount of money spares you a 500-day wait and multiple rounds of public review.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says very likely, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is an open question; second, much of the burden is not paperwork at all — it is mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split food spending — the kind of question AI struggles to answer for you too. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years is convinced AI will help enormously.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose roughly fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey does not accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and the rise in obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants must submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both directions — about paying people who do not need it, and about denying people who genuinely do — so she does not think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her off her UBI position
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering", and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialise. Her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and would not go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and UBI-type policies would have to be considered.
