To capture every detail she could perceive, Tannen annotated the transcript with the difference between the pronunciations of the and the, measured the seconds of perceptible pause with a stopwatch, and then had the participants themselves listen to the recording to check. It was precisely this precision that let her see: a New Yorker's ‘interruption’ is sometimes an expression of enthusiasm, not rudeness. From this she proposed a counterintuitive mechanism — an interruption is completed by two people: one starts talking, the other stops, and it is the latter who defines ‘talking at the same time’ as an interruption.

10:21 The more urgently you yield the floor, the more silent the other person gets
In the recording Tannen heard an embarrassing side of herself: she calls it machine gun questions. To be friendly to Chuck, a guest from Los Angeles, and hand him the floor, she fired off questions in rapid succession — you live in LA? Here visiting? What do you do there? What do you do at Disney, a writer? An artist? You write ad copy? She already knew the answers; she just wanted to give him an opening. It backfired: Chuck was caught off guard by the speed of the questions and, instead of picking up the thread, went quieter. She realized that the more she asked, the more urgently she asked — she was machine-gunning him.

20:48 Beating around the bush is asking ‘he cares’
Why not just say what you want? Tannen uses birthday gifts to explain: you want the person who loves you to give you the gift you want, because that proves they care, that they were willing to go to the trouble of guessing, that they know you well enough. If you tell them outright, you get the gift but not the things you actually wanted — ‘he cares’, ‘he gets you’. Indirect expression works the same way in other settings. She also corrects a common attribution: this is not always a male-female difference; between her and her Greek husband, it is she who is more direct and he who is more indirect; region, ethnicity and culture all shape style.

36:41 Only people with power can afford to beat around the bush
A career naval officer told Tannen that this is how the military works: when he was still a cadet, the instructor walked into the classroom and said ‘it's a little cold in here’, everyone nodded, and the instructor said ‘when I say something, I expect you to do something about it — one more time — it's a little cold in here’, at which point everyone jumped up to close the windows. Tannen's conclusion is that it is precisely because he has power that the instructor enjoys the luxury of indirect expression. The same sentence — ‘could you grab me that report update’ — is heard by one person as the boss not pulling rank and treating me as one of his own, and by another as the boss being too soft, why doesn't he just give the order.

47:16 Treating good intentions as the default is a rhetorical strategy
Tannen calls her own position ‘a rhetoric of good intentions’. People often push back: what if the other person really is malicious? Her response is — that's not news. People are already ready at any moment to see others as ill-intentioned and personally flawed. The news her work can offer is this: step back and consider that the other person may not be malicious, just has a different conversational style and is pursuing his positive goals in a different way. Thinking about conversational style gives you a channel for imagining different intentions.

1:12:22 Silence is not a compromise, it loses on both ends
On ‘lies of omission’, Emma Levine points out that the speaker's and the listener's judgments are completely misaligned. The speaker feels silence is a moral compromise: more moral than lying, less moral than telling the truth. But the listener can see through your avoidance, and what he usually wants is comfort, affirmation, to feel a little better. If you turn away or change the subject, he neither hears the truth nor gets the social goal of being loved and affirmed — so silence is sometimes not a compromise but the worst option, stripping away both kindness and honesty at once.

1:32:03 Whether you dare tell the truth is decided by context
Research by Emma Levine and Yenna Kim and others compared critical feedback in the US and China: in China, people are more willing to give critical feedback, because both sides share an understanding of what the norm is and where things fall short, and criticism is seen as a shared responsibility; in the US, the default is ‘you do you’ — what right do I have to comment on your workplace behavior. Levine's conclusion is that whether you dare tell the truth is not a matter of personality but is determined by context and cultural components.

item.title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rewriting it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-cn18b4d2-ai-原生组织不是人人用-ai-是假设组织不存在重写一遍/
item.description: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder type in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool and the right to allocate it, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
item.content:encoded:
Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder type in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool and the right to allocate it, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.

The founder of a 12-year hardware company explains the concrete mechanics of rewriting an organization: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pitfalls.

4:01 AI-native starts by assuming the organization doesn't exist
Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a single founder starting a company to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes, it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

6:04 HARO's head comes from technology, not HR
Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT: the head must understand the business, and the person chosen is an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR head leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person runs it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder work) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

10:04 Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line, map out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover both; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their day jobs. The company also set up AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI 起航员’ (AI navigators) and above that ‘领航员’ (pilots).

16:06 Circles erase functional power; the circle lead gets the bonus pool
Lockin's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is a dual line of product line and function, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first half year to a year of the change, the front line gets to decide.

20:36 Experience can become a burden instead
Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear about doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the worst is the half-informed — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel they are very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as their foundation, but on which processes and which roles can be removed, the clear-eyed judge more easily. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill with skills and building Agents; only L3 can author workflows.

23:23 R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
Chen Bin admits the speed of transformation varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, since writing code every day gives immediate positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and a bigger bonus. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and 60-point output doesn't stick around. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content brings conversion is the standard.

35:32 Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, then sit down again
Lockin ran three internal rounds of sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level ten or twenty Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and the talks for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may finally be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

42:16 To hire, you must first prove AI can't do the job
After people from the original departments are picked off by circles, when a boss wants to add headcount there are logically only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain clearly why a management trainee won't do and why AI won't do. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, working with Chen Bin on the AI-native transformation.

item.title: He Unlocked the Chains of the Mentally Ill, Then Forged Psychological Ones
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-stuffmissed-他解开了精神病人的锁链-却造出了心理锁链/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a single year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.
item.content:encoded:
Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a single year, mostly through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.

A crossover case of medical history and social reform, suited to anyone who wants to see how a humanitarian reform gets amplified by institutions; but the controversy only arrives in the back half, and the early biography is flat.

4:07 No license is what forced the case-file system into existence
The medical degree Pinel earned in Toulouse only allowed him to practice in Toulouse, so after arriving in Montpellier and then Paris he could not practice directly. During his four years in Montpellier he instead visited hospitals repeatedly, talked with patients at length, and took copious notes, organizing the information into detailed records. Because he tracked the same patients over a long period, he could observe how illnesses evolved and thereby identify patterns in their course. This ‘observe—record—track’ method was later carried to Bicêtre, where it became the prototype for building a file on every patient, recording age, temperature, diagnosis, and even comparing patients' body temperatures against the building's temperature.

8:19 Classifying the mentally ill with plant taxonomy
The seventh ward at Bicêtre held 200 men judged to be mentally deranged, many chained in extremely small rooms, with chains long enough only to let them shuffle around inside. Pinel communicated closely with the director, Jean-Baptiste Poussin, gathered as much patient information as possible, organized it into tables, and transferred his knowledge of plant classification over to the problem, trying to build finer diagnostic categories rather than simply lumping people together as ‘mad.’ He did not call patients ‘mad’ or ‘mentally ill’ but said they were in a state of ‘mental alienation’—that is, estranged from their own reason.

9:21 Mortality fell from 50% to under 13%
Pinel put a concrete set of practices in place at Bicêtre: moving patients out of prison-style confinement and into rooms with as much natural light as possible; no longer using chaining as a routine measure; establishing hygiene standards for the institution; having patients take regular hot baths; and providing what today would be called occupational therapy to help patients overcome the obstacles of daily life. Within a year, the institution's annual patient mortality rate fell from 50% to under 13%. The show states plainly that this was largely just a matter of keeping patients and their environment clean—where disease is spreading, without cleanliness there is no control. In addition, a considerable share of patients were able to return to life outside the institution, whereas at the time the expectation for most people entering an asylum was to die inside it.

19:43 He measured skulls to prove phrenology was garbage
Pinel recorded age, temperature and diagnosis for every patient, and also measured skulls. This was not because he believed in phrenology—quite the opposite: phrenology was just taking shape during his main working period, built on the craniology that originated in Austria in the 1790s, which held that the shape of a head revealed whether a person was inclined to violence or madness. Pinel considered the whole thing useless, and he collected skull measurements precisely in order to falsify it. He later wrote that the data seemed to confirm his earlier view: strong mental emotions are the most common cause of mental derangement, and the skulls of the insane have no special formation that cannot be found in any other skull picked at random.

21:46 He did not unlock everyone's chains
The image of ‘Pinel breaking all his patients' chains and turning prisoners into patients’ needs discounting. A famous late-19th-century painting by Tony Robert-Fleury depicts him removing chains, and it shows the women's institution. But he did not release every patient bound in irons: where he judged that loosening them would create danger, patients remained confined and tethered. In the paper he read in 1794 he gave several cases of men he called ‘agitated and violent,’ one of whom had been chained for more than forty years. He described their behavior in detail to explain why irons were needed, and wrote that one of the basic principles for dealing with the mentally deranged is ‘a judicious mixture of affability and firmness,’ avoiding unnecessary coercion and using only as much force as is needed to restrain them.

27:53 He denied brain pathology, and that is a real flaw
One long-standing criticism of Pinel's work is that he ignored the physiological causes of mental health problems. His writing discusses at length how life events worsen mental conditions, yet never considers bodily causes—which is strange, because writing on the physiological causes of mental illness goes back to Hippocrates and Galen, and in Pinel's own time Lavoisier, along with his university colleague Michel-Augustin Theret, were already discussing brain chemistry. In 1801 Pinel explicitly argued against bodily causes of madness, writing that ‘the derangement of the understanding is generally considered as the result of an organic lesion of the brain, and consequently as incurable; a supposition that is, in a great number of instances, contrary to anatomical fact.’ The show says directly: he was completely wrong on this point.

30:56 The ‘Citizen, I am convinced’ story may be invented
In 1849 Chambers' Edinburgh Journal published a story about Pinel, sourced to Pinel's son Scipion Pinel—who also became a psychiatrist. The story goes that during the Terror, a Paris Commune official, Georges Coudon, came to Bicêtre hunting for ‘traitors feigning madness,’ and after seeing the chains, the filth and the mad howling with his own eyes, asked Pinel whether it was he who was mad for wanting to unchain these people. Pinel is said to have replied: ‘Citizen, I am convinced that these madmen have become so unmanageable only because they have been deprived of air and liberty.’ The show says this sounds very cool and very clever, but whether the story is true, we don't know—it may be family legend, or it may have been made up by an editor. It certainly added a brick to Pinel's 19th-century legend.

32:59 Foucault: iron chains were swapped for psychological ones
Pinel's writing and work have been argued over almost continuously for nearly two hundred years. Supporters point out how progressive his work was and how many of his ideas remain relevant today. One particularly forceful critic was the 20th-century philosopher Michel Foucault. Foucault argued that Pinel may have removed the physical shackles from patients, but only replaced them with psychological shackles, describing his work as a kind of ‘moral imprisonment’ in which patients were manipulated in more subtle forms during treatment. By Foucault's logic, in becoming obedient to the doctor, patients became estranged from themselves. The show also notes that this line of argument in Foucault has problems of its own.

item.title: Charged Black Holes Emit Charged Particles, and Quantum Gravity Corrections Barely Matter
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-instituteforad-带电黑洞发射带电粒子-量子引力修正几乎不起作用/
item.description: Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.
item.content:encoded:
Quantum corrections to near-extremal black holes drastically rewrite the Hawking spectrum for photons and gravitons, but switch to charged particles and the corrections nearly vanish — because the particles are mostly produced in the throat, far from the horizon, where they cannot feel the metric fluctuations near the horizon.

A high-energy theory session: derivation-dense, high terminology barrier; listen if you are interested in black hole information and quantum gravity, otherwise the information density is on the low side.

1:20 Near-extremal black holes are actually quantum objects
In classical general relativity a black hole is characterized by three parameters — mass M, charge Q, angular momentum J — and solutions exist only when M is greater than or equal to Q; the case of exact equality is an extremal black hole, and close to equality is a near-extremal black hole. Over the past few years, via the Euclidean gravitational path integral, it was discovered that near-extremal black holes receive very large fluctuations from the quantum metric, and many textbook properties are thereby rewritten. This is precisely the motivation for this talk: since so many properties have changed, the standard story of Hawking radiation should be run through again too.

10:29 The Schwarzian mode is one-loop exact
Write the metric as a classical solution plus fluctuations and the gauge field as a classical field plus fluctuations, then expand the action, and you can compute the fluctuations. In the past this was done only at quadratic order, to compute the logarithmic correction to the entropy; the new development is the identification of a special class of metric fluctuations confined deep in the ADS2 throat, namely the Schwarzian modes. Their effective action is proportional to temperature divided by some energy scale, vanishes at zero temperature, and contributes enormously when the temperature is far below that scale. More crucially, this action as a whole is the Schwarzian theory, and it is one-loop exact: computing only the quadratic term automatically includes all higher-order interaction terms.

20:50 The neutral-particle spectrum is rewritten by quantum corrections
For the S-wave of a massless scalar, the Hawking formula gives the energy flux. Taking the initial energy to be 100 times the breaking scale, the quantum rate and the semiclassical curve nearly coincide; but pushing the initial energy down to one tenth of the breaking scale, the two curves diverge enormously, and the quantum rate does not allow the black hole to radiate away more energy than the amount by which it exceeds extremality. This is the evidence that quantum gravity corrections matter in the neutral-particle story, and it is the benchmark against which charged particles are to be compared.

26:56 Charged particles were previously uncomputable because the dimension goes complex
In parameter space, in the region where both mass and charge are large (the QED region) as well as in the massless charged region, the scaling dimension of a scalar field in ADS2 becomes complex, the techniques used for neutral particles do not apply, and this is why charged particles long remained incompletely understood. The only corner where similar techniques carry over is the ‘lightly charged field’ corner: add a tiny charge to a massless field so that the particle charge times the black hole charge is far less than 1, and the scaling dimension is about 1. In this corner, adding a little charge makes the deviation from the semiclassical answer shrink dramatically.

33:27 The Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation are equivalent
There are two perspectives in the literature for computing black hole electron production: one is Hawking-style, canonically quantizing on a curved background and evaluating the particle number operator at infinity; the other is Schwinger-style, treating the black hole as a background electric field and computing pair production via the Schwinger mechanism. The former is the correct computation and implicitly contains Schwinger pair production, but it is extremely hard; the latter is far easier. This talk proves that as the temperature goes to zero, the Hawking computation and the Schwinger computation give nearly identical results, the only difference being that Hawking decomposes into spherical-angular-momentum modes with quantized angular momentum, whereas Schwinger uses a flat-space approximation with no quantized angular momentum.

43:34 A single electron kicks the black hole back into the safe zone
The backreaction is very violent: if the black hole sits in the near-extremal, highly quantized region, then emitting just one electron (which carries away a large amount of energy and charge) leaves the black hole in a final state that falls back into the completely safe semiclassical region. This explains why quantum gravity corrections to charged-particle emission do not matter — the produced particle itself pushes the system out of the quantum region.

50:38 The superradiance boundary is where particles just barely cannot escape
Reinterpreting the Hawking spectrum in the Schwinger picture, it splits into three segments. Near the superradiance boundary (the green region): in the point-particle approximation, a particle produced too close to the horizon falls in and cannot escape, so the rate drops sharply to zero at the superradiance boundary; the peak corresponds exactly to the position of the point particle's unstable minimum, push it a little to the left and it escapes, a little to the right and it falls into the black hole. The middle purple region: particles are produced in the long ADS2 throat or in the flat-space part, and Schwinger is an excellent approximation. The leftmost red region: particles would have to be produced at infinity in an infinitely weak electric field, the rate is essentially zero, and so an essential singularity appears.

53:38 Quantum corrections cannot reach most of the particles
In a certain gauge the metric fluctuations are localized near the Euclidean horizon, whereas charged particles are mostly produced in the throat or even farther out in the flat-space region, far from these fluctuations, unable to feel them, so the rate is naturally unaffected. What might receive large corrections is the green region hugging the superradiance boundary, but that region is small and its contribution to the total rate is limited. The author states explicitly that tools are currently lacking to compute precisely how the green-region rate is modified, so no precise answer can be given.

item.title: Obeying Incentives Is for Losers: You Should Decide Right and Wrong for Yourself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-econtalk-遵守激励是失败者行为-你该自己判断对错/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-econtalk-遵守激励是失败者行为-你该自己判断对错/
item.description: Economists say fix the incentives and you fix the world. Mastroianni says that misses half of it: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. Outsourcing your value judgments to an incentive structure is abandoning the core task of being a person.
item.content:encoded:
Economists say fix the incentives and you fix the world. Mastroianni says that misses half of it: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. Outsourcing your value judgments to an incentive structure is abandoning the core task of being a person.

Medium information density; the early stretch gets tangled up in Omelas and Rube Goldberg, and the real stuff is the big fish, Sumner, and high pay selecting the wrong people in the middle and back half.

8:07 Having a reason to do wrong doesn't mean you should
Mastroianni first grants that incentive analysis beats "people do bad things because they're bad": at least it admits people have reasons, and changing the reasons can change the behavior. But he adds a premise economists often miss — if you do it because an external reward structure tells you it's good, because it will pat you on the head or give you a little treat, that's loser behavior. His words: even if you have a reason to do something bad, you still shouldn't do it. He jokes that this is an obvious point, but some points are so obvious that nobody thinks to say them.

12:21 The real Omelas is a Rube Goldberg machine
In Le Guin's Omelas, the whole city's happiness rests on a tortured child in the basement, and some people choose to walk away. Mastroianni says that story was in his head when he wrote the piece, but he cut a section: in the story you have some metaphysical connection to the child, whereas in reality the connection is more like a Rube Goldberg machine — you aren't the one torturing the child, you're three warehouses away, just the hammer that swings down, hits the ball, the ball rolls down the slope, lights the match. The bad thing is far from you, you didn't do it with your own hands, but you're in the causal chain. That makes "walking away" much harder and far less heroic: it doesn't look like brushing the dust of Omelas off your feet, it looks like "I'm not going to be VP of brand partnerships for Philip Morris."

17:27 Outsourcing value judgment means being conscripted by the wicked
Russ asks: are you saying we should encourage people to be more moral? Mastroianni says he doesn't think that can be centrally organized, demanded, mandated or cultivated by government — when government tries, it tends to go bad fast. His goal is to produce the kind of person who does the right thing even when it's inconvenient, even when it's costly. He offers a chain: if you only do what's rewarded, you can start out amoral and end up deputized for the immoral. His judgment: the wicked are few; what's plentiful is people with no strong sense of right and wrong, and those people can be turned into an army by the wicked.

20:33 The big fish will find you; you decide whether to look
"Big fish" comes from Lovecraft's Dagon: a man sees a fish god, is never right again for the rest of his life, and finally jumps out a window. Mastroianni uses it as a metaphor — everyone has a fish inside them, and if you really take it seriously you have to overturn your entire life. His own fish was the 2020 Society for Personality and Social Psychology conference in San Francisco: the venue was in the Tenderloin, and inside people nibbled canapés and talked about reducing implicit bias a tiny bit, possibly just noise, while outside people curled up with fentanyl in their veins. He specifically brings up the 1970s seminary student experiment: randomly assign students to speak on the Good Samaritan or on career opportunities, then randomly tell them they're late or on time, and the only thing that determines whether they stop for the man lying by the road is whether they're in a hurry. He says this is one of the most famous findings in the field, everyone in that room knew it, and nobody felt any conflict over it — that was the fish he saw.

31:28 Sumner went back to provoking after being caned
Charles Sumner is the man whose statue Mastroianni walked past every day in grad school. He came from a poor Boston family, his father was illegitimate; the place where he grew up was home to large numbers of formerly enslaved people. He went to France, and at the Sorbonne he saw Black and white students studying together as equals, and wrote in his diary: the difference between people is obviously not caused by nature, it can only be caused by education. He became a radical abolitionist, arguing not just for abolition but for racially integrated schools and Black suffrage — things that only became common sense more than a century later. As a senator he gave a fierce anti-slavery speech, and days later a Southern congressman walked up to his desk and beat him nearly to death with a cane; he was trapped in the desk, soaking in his own blood, and took more than a year to recover. After recovering he kept provoking, and pushed Lincoln to issue the Emancipation Proclamation two years early. His new biographer says Sumner is cited 40 times in the brief for Brown v. Board.

40:20 Desperate to join the club of people you don't respect
Russ cites Adam Smith: we want to be loved and to be lovely, so we should surround ourselves with good people whose approval we want. Mastroianni goes harder: he and the people close to him have spent their whole lives desperately seeking opportunities from people they don't respect, landing them in an absurd position — "I think they're bad people, I think they're completely wrong about what's good and bad, but I really want them to let me into their club." Into it to do what? You will inevitably become more like them; you can't help it. He says the moment you can say "I distrust this person's judgment so much that even though he could give me success, I'll go do something else" — that's the moment of freedom he described earlier: that person has no more power over you.

50:15 High pay doesn't buy you better professors
Russ says he made about $18,600 a year when he graduated, and is glad he didn't go into finance or a big company's chief economist office. He asks: economics professors can make $500,000 or even $750,000 a year — when there's that much money, are the norms that founded the discipline, honesty and truth-seeking, harder to maintain? Mastroianni says this looks more like a selection effect than a corruption effect: the people attracted by $750,000 are often not the people who can be good professors; the consequence of high pay isn't corrupting people who might have been good, it's attracting people who shouldn't be there and making them compete with each other. Russ presses: doesn't paying $750,000 get you the best professors? Mastroianni answers: the professor you want is someone who puts truth above everything, and once the money is big enough, the people who come are the ones who don't put truth first — and our selection procedures can't tell who's in it for truth and who's in it for the salary, especially since many of the people doing the selecting came for the wrong reasons themselves.

57:37 Status is harder to separate from knowledge than money is
Mastroianni says that in most places it isn't money that attracts the wrong people, it's status: being called professor feels good, so many people want it, so few get it. And status markers are harder to distinguish from knowledge markers than money markers are, because they claim to be knowledge markers themselves — "you published in a good journal, so it must be good work." He says we've now reached the point where people talk about writing a specific paper for a specific journal, and call papers pubs or A-pubs; he finds it vile and disgusting, like defiling a cross. He says this is why he isn't in academia: he's willing to earn less to study what he thinks matters, to put up with job insecurity, to move around the world — but if after all that it's still "why don't you publish a pile of garbage papers" and "why don't you massage the statistics a little," then it isn't worth it.

item.title: OpenAI Declares the AGI Era, but There Isn't Enough Compute to Go Around
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-a16z-openai-宣布进入-agi-时代-但算力不够分给所有人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-a16z-openai-宣布进入-agi-时代-但算力不够分给所有人/
item.description: Greg Brockman says Astra can run coherently for 24 hours on a task, so you can reasonably call it AGI; the real bottleneck isn't model capability but compute and safety alignment — no matter how strong the model gets, it may not reach everyone cheaply.
item.content:encoded:
Greg Brockman says Astra can run coherently for 24 hours on a task, so you can reasonably call it AGI; the real bottleneck isn't model capability but compute and safety alignment — no matter how strong the model gets, it may not reach everyone cheaply.

Greg rarely talks about how OpenAI internally uses 10,000 agents to solve math problems, how it killed Sora, and how it pulls 25% of production engineers into defense — the mechanism details are worth more than the conclusions.

0:00 AGI isn't a moment, it's a blurry spectrum
Greg says AGI is no longer a point in time but a blurry spectrum. His judgment is that Astra has already ‘hit something’ and can reasonably be called AGI: it can use a computer, take on long-horizon tasks, and OpenAI has seen it run coherently for 24 hours straight to finish a task, across a very broad range of domains. But he stresses the model is still jagged — writing is ‘the first time it's not slop’, but it still isn't good; in some places just a little more polish would make it great, and right now it's just short of that. He cites the jagged-boundary diagram from Twitter and says the place you actually want to get to is stability across every dimension, not exceptional strength in a few.

4:08 Not enough compute: a strong model still can't reach everyone
Greg frames ‘pacing the frontier’ as two things: one is model capability itself, which he believes is achievable; the other is distributing that capability to everyone, which he calls the massively underrated challenge. In his words the model will be strong enough, but ‘we won't have enough compute to serve it all’ — it's hard to deliver it to everyone in an affordable way. He also calls safety, security and alignment almost the bottleneck on progress — not something you patch after the model is done, but a standard you must continuously up-level, or it becomes the thing holding back the schedule.

9:25 The Hugging Face incident is the alarm clock for the defense window
Greg splits the Hugging Face incident into two layers: one is how OpenAI itself monitors, sandboxes and controls models during evals, which made the team change a large number of internal standards; the other is that it previewed what broad capability diffusion into the hands of threat actors looks like — an AI that can both escape a secure environment and hack into a company's production environment, and what it found was quite sophisticated. His conclusion is that defenders have a window right now: frontier capability is still in the hands of a few companies, defenders have differential access, and they should use this time to raise their own security waterline with frontier models, so that when capability diffuses they get pulled up along with it. Ben Horowitz adds the flip side: we have 50 years of code and architecture that wasn't designed for this world, plus a pile of consumer-data honeypots sitting on the internet.

12:31 10,000 agents cracked Navier-Stokes
Ben raises the upside: you can deploy 10,000 agents, let them communicate with each other and self-organize to do work. Greg confirms OpenAI used 10,000 agents to attack the Navier-Stokes problem, and formalized it in Lean so the AI writes verifiable code. He gives the significance two layers: the problem itself has applications in fluid dynamics and ocean currents; more importantly it represents AI creating new knowledge, which could open a whole wave of scientific and drug discovery. That connects to what he says later about ‘formally verifying all software’ — something that never took off because it was too infeasible for humans, and now that AI has proof capability, it becomes possible again.

13:32 OpenAI pulls 25% of production engineers to play defense
Greg describes OpenAI's own approach: pull 25% of production engineers off their projects, tell them everything is paused, and that their job now is defense — using models to find holes in their own systems. They found a batch of serious issues and fixed them. He also describes a convergence process: point Astra at your own systems, find new problems, but eventually it saturates — Astra is smart enough that it has basically found all the P0s it can find, and then you wait for the next, stronger model to open a new round. From this he proposes the ‘defense factory’: end-to-end automation from vulnerability discovery, triage, fix, deployment to verification, and if you can do it at machine speed, defenders gain a very large advantage.

18:47 Codex found 13 vulnerabilities in 15 minutes
Greg gives the example of his own site, gregbrockman.com: a very simple static site, and he had Codex do a penetration test. It came back in 15 minutes with 13 findings — an SPF record set up so someone could forge email, some requests going over HTTP without forcing HTTPS, and so on. Individually none of them is a big deal, but he says if AI can chain many small vulnerabilities into one big one, that's different. Then he had Codex just fix them: over 45 minutes it opened cloud service consoles, clicked around, set various headers, migrated to Cloudflare Pages, and kicked off the DMARC process (with a 48-hour window). He says after those 45 minutes he felt ‘so protected’.

30:07 US AI sentiment is lowest because nobody tells people the upside
Ben asks why AI sentiment in Asia and Europe is higher than in the US. Greg's answer: the industry and companies need to do a better job explaining to people ‘why you benefit’, not just that this is a strategic asset for the country. He offers a set of usage numbers: ChatGPT has roughly 1.1 billion weekly active users, about 100 million in the US, close to a third of the population using it weekly. He tells a friend's story: she was in the hospital, the doctor was about to inject some antibiotic, she typed a question to ChatGPT, and ChatGPT said absolutely do not use that — you had that condition a year ago and it could be fatal; she showed the response to the doctor, who said that's exactly right, I only have five minutes to read your chart. Greg says stories like this aren't told enough and need to enter the public consciousness.

43:50 Killing Sora was about getting the business moving
Greg says this year's theme is focus, because ‘we can't do it all’. The test is to reason backward from the mission: if deployment and productization strengthen the mission, keep it; if not, cut it. He states plainly that Sora was the highest-profile of the canceled projects, and ‘very painful’, but it had to happen to unblock the business. Another move was merging the consumer and enterprise chat into chat work. He admits that in the first half many metrics were pointing the wrong way, and the team had to be told repeatedly to get back to basics, quoting “The Score Takes Care of Itself”: you can't affect the outcome, only the inputs, and winning the Super Bowl comes down to blocking and tackling. His own focus over the past two years has shifted from data centers, infrastructure and ML engineering to the business this year.

item.title: After AI Takes the Talent, Only Six Tokens Are Left in Crypto
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-14-empire-ai-抢走人才后-加密的机会只剩六种代币/
