He judges this wave of ‘chipmaxing’ will be one of the most far-reaching technology transitions in semiconductor history, roughly on the scale of the move to 300 mm wafers.

8:12 The spot market has vanished, and VCs now hunt GPUs for their portfolio
When the author was last in the Bay Area in September 2025 the picture was completely different. Since then long-running agentic AI has swept Silicon Valley, triggered in part by stronger models such as Anthropic's Opus 4.5 around November 2025 and by Open Claw. In February 2026 prices began to rise, everyone scrambled to lock up compute, and Anthropic led the way signing big deals with SpaceX, Google and others. The author was told that by the time of this trip the spot market had completely disappeared. For Neoclouds (a term coined by semi-analyst Dan Nishbal in April 2024 for pure cloud vendors that resell AI training and inference compute, such as Coreweave and Nebius) this is a huge boon, and they are confident the shortage will last at least another one to two years. The author met several people who did not know each other and each wanted to start a Neocloud. For AI startups this is a business risk: imagine telling investors the product has to wait until mid-2027 because there is not enough compute. The new way VCs help their portfolio companies is to go find compute, and he heard of people scraping together a thousand GPUs and even hunting in unexpected places like Eastern Europe.

9:12 Two giants are feasting while compute is still being wasted
By contrast, Anthropic and OpenAI are feasting internally. Dylan recently said on Dashpod that these two AI giants each have about 5 GW of compute. The author infers from this that a substantial share of all that compute may be wasted, and anecdotes he heard confirm that this ‘rolling in it’ state is not being used as efficiently as possible. He also asked every AI insider he talked to one question: will Google return to the frontier? The general consensus is no, though the explanations are vague. Several people pointed out that Google's decision to sell a large amount of compute to Anthropic is itself a sign that it does not believe it either. This is a big reversal from the period when Gemini 3 made some people think OpenAI was finished. What the author heard is that Google suffered serious talent drain, plus a culture unfriendly to frontier AI.

11:15 Neolabs are venture capital that treats compute as money
What fascinates the author most is the Neolab: a research startup with basically no revenue that raises money to explore an interesting AI idea, whose founders are often elite researchers and whose business plan is little more than ‘discover a completely new architecture’. The most famous and earliest, Safe Superintelligence, raised a billion dollars and has still released no product or model. The label is fuzzy, covering recursive intelligence, Humans, Core Automation, Flapping Airplanes and others; among those with products are Japan's Sakana AI, Thinking Machines, Reflection AI, plus a batch in verticals such as materials science, world models and robotics. The first reaction is that these assets are dumb: no revenue, no plan to monetize soon. But the author can understand it: historically breakthrough science came from research universities, government labs or Bell Labs, and now university funding is being cut and talent is being sucked into industry; AI is probably the first major technology in the past 50 years to emerge without government involvement, and in this era research is closed and secretive. So let Nvidia, with compute and cash in hand, plus a pile of VCs, fund these asymmetric bets. OpenAI and Anthropic are locked into the transformer paradigm and are unlikely to spend on researching these directions. The failure probability is high, but most of the money was given in the form of compute anyway; if someone really strikes gold and forces the giants to pivot (say, to a more data-efficient architecture), the giants will most likely buy the discoverer at an eye-watering price, and one such deal pays for everything. The author thinks this is a better use of cash than continuing buybacks, and names Apple.

14:15 Tokens are burning, and nobody has measured ROI
Customers really are burning tokens, but are they getting ROI? The author asked across the ecosystem and the answer remains vague: don't know, nobody has measured it, it is all anecdote. He believes lower barriers to coding will hit knowledge work — financial firms used to hire a pile of reporting analysts to keep management on top of positions, and now two smart young analysts plus Claude writing a dashboard is enough, which he has seen with his own eyes. But for other AI capabilities, such as making spreadsheets or making presentations, the things marketing usually pushes, he has seen no obvious impact. Maybe it just needs more time, maybe it is a problem of intelligence itself. OpenAI recently published a blog on how agents accelerate internal research, but still positions AI's capability at intern level: it can execute routine tasks, and is far from a real AI researcher. What he heard is that AI still lacks human research taste, though some believe sufficient scale can achieve it. And one thing holds for everyone in San Francisco: people are working harder than before. If the models are really that capable, why does everyone say they have more work? Maybe AI does not kill our work for us, but gives us more work.

15:17 In 2027 compute flips from shortage to glut
Everyone says shortage, shortage, two more years of shortage, and the author instead suspects things will not go as expected. His arithmetic is not complicated: usable AI data center capacity at the end of 2026 is estimated at about 15 GW, with OpenAI and Anthropic each taking about 5 GW; the supply chain will respond, and by the end of 2027 that number is estimated to race to 45-55 GW, an increment of 30-40 GW, of which the two giants take about 30 GW. Assume half goes to training, leaving 15 GW combined for inference for the two. Currently each gigawatt of inference is modeled as bringing in about $50 billion of revenue (this number comes from Dylan Patel on Dashpod), and it can also be back-solved from Anthropic's deal to buy 300 MW from SpaceX for $1.25 billion a month; Dylan thinks smarter models can eventually push it to $100 billion per gigawatt. On that math, in 2027 the two should produce $750 billion to $1.5 trillion of revenue. The author says that number is too absurd: most people agree the two will do $150-200 billion this year, and next year he can barely imagine $400-500 billion, but $750 billion to $1.5 trillion is ‘two Walmarts’ or ‘two Toyotas’, a credibility stretch, and he does not think it can be reached. He bets revenue per gigawatt is far below $100 billion or even $50 billion, possibly only a small fraction of it. From the infrastructure side it looks the same: assume 40 GW lands in 2027, current rent is about $20 million per megawatt, corresponding to a 3-year payback, so those 40 GW require $800 billion paid to infrastructure providers, in 2027 alone. He does not think that can be collected either, which means rents have to fall and someone somewhere has to take a loss. Conclusion: in 2027 the supply chain will deliver a lot of compute, most of it in the second half, and he bets this pushes the market from shortage to glut. He stresses he is not saying the AI bubble will pop, only that we will soon be flooded with compute — 2026 is agentic demand matched against 2025 supply, supply will catch up and probably overshoot; but after that maybe the next stage of growth ignites and demand balloons again, for example persistent AI.

item.title: Stalin Was Just the Bookkeeper of the Revolution, and Then He Became General Secretary
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-empirehist-斯大林在革命里只是个管账的-后来却成了总书记/
item.description: In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by speeches, but by sitting at the table.
item.content:encoded:
In 1917, while Lenin and Trotsky were on the streets calling for insurrection, Stalin was doing the organizing and fundraising nobody else wanted. He became General Secretary later not by speeches, but by sitting at the table.

This episode covers the groundwork before Stalin took power: Georgian origins, seminary, a failed bank robbery. Medium information density, but it makes clear why he was able to rise.

5:28 Even his birthday was something he changed himself
The parish register, the seminary certificate, the tsarist police file and his own handwritten questionnaire from the 1920s all say 18 December 1878. But the birthday he announced after taking power was 21 December 1879 — one year and three days off. Bob Service offers one judgment in his biography: forgery was too easy for him. Service also has an unprovable but persuasive conjecture — that changing his birthday helped him dodge conscription when he was young. The thing itself is the theme of the whole episode: this man's attitude toward facts was instrumental.

6:35 How anomalous it was for a Georgian to become master of Moscow
His real name was Joseph Jugashvili, and he was born in Georgia. Georgia is in the Caucasus, next to Armenia, just north of Iran and Turkey, very far from Russia; it has its own language, its own alphabet, and its religion is Georgian Orthodoxy, which is not the same thing as Russian Orthodoxy. The analogy the episode gives is this: a man of Georgian Orthodox background climbing to the top of power in Moscow is equivalent to a man of Irish Catholic background from some remote place like Limerick becoming master of London in the mid-20th century. For Georgians at the time, being ruled from Moscow meant being colonized.

8:43 His father refused to change trades, and then started hitting people
His father Bessarion (nicknamed Besso) was a cobbler with his own workshop in Gori, and by most accounts a good craftsman. But he refused to keep up with the times: he kept making Georgian-style soft leather high boots while the market had already shifted to European shoes. He did not adapt; he became bitter, drank heavily, and the violence fell mainly on his wife Ekaterina (Kiki) and little Joseph, who was nicknamed "Crazy Besso." Stalin later told his daughter Svetlana one scene: his father was drunk and beating his mother, he grabbed a knife and threw it at his father, missed, his father charged at him, and he ran to a neighbor's house and hid there for several days until his father's rage passed.

11:52 Smallpox, a carriage, and a left arm that was too short
Around age six he caught smallpox, severe enough that his mother thought he would die — two older brothers had already died in infancy, and the family was too poor to afford a doctor, so they could only call a local folk healer. He survived, but his face was permanently scarred, and every official photograph was retouched. Later a runaway carriage hit him and broke his arm; the left arm never healed properly and was visibly shorter and stiffer for the rest of his life. As the episode puts it: smallpox did not take him, his father's violence did not take him, and the carriage did not take him either. His mother was extremely devoted to him and had ambitious plans for him.

16:07 He wrote poetry, and he was good at it
In his late teens two things happened at once: he began writing quite good poetry, and he entered the seminary. The episode reads one poem: "The pink buds have already blossomed, toward the pale violet violets; brushed by the breeze, the lily of the valley bends down over the grass. Flowers, my Georgia. May peace come to my native land, and may you, friends, make our homeland famous through study." Anita says that in the original Georgian it is quite beautiful. It shows two things: he was a proud Georgian, not a Russian; and in the tsarist context, this way of writing about a "homeland" was already close to sedition.

19:09 The seminary was the tsar's Russification machine
In 1894 he won a place at the Tiflis Theological Seminary. The sign over the door said Georgian Orthodox, but the school was in fact under the control of the Russian Orthodox Church, one of the institutions the tsar used to "Russify" the borderlands. Students were kept under close surveillance, and reports were written constantly: were these people good tsarist subjects, were they talking sedition. And right under that surveillance, he was reading banned books, including What Is to Be Done? and other big questions about freedom and the individual. Anita's comment in the episode is: the surveillance here was not done well enough.

21:11 He gave himself the name of a bandit
On the banned list was a Georgian novel, Alexander Kazbegi's The Patricide, whose protagonist is a mountain fugitive named Koba. He took that name as his own alias, and at the seminary his classmates called him by it. The episode calls this a kind of "name determinism": he first took the name of a bandit hero, and then he really did become a bandit. The turning point from seminary student to bandit began when he saw with his own eyes two mountain bandits publicly hanged in the center of Gori for shooting a policeman over a stray cow — he was forbidden to go watch, but he went.

24:16 They robbed 250,000 rubles and could not spend a single one
In 1907 he and a group of friends ambushed a bank carriage in Yerevan Square in Tiflis, almost within sight of the seminary: some stood on high ground throwing bombs down, others fired in the street, and the man organizing, financing and directing it all behind the scenes was Stalin, alias Koba. They got away with 250,000 rubles packed in linen sacks. But the bank had already published the serial numbers of its largest-denomination notes, so not one ruble of the money could be spent. It was the first time he left a police photograph on file, but he did not go to prison for it and essentially walked away untouched.

item.title: Outbound reply rates near zero? Don't blame the copy yet — check who you're sending to first
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ycsp-外联回复率接近零-先别怪文案-先查你在发给谁/
item.description: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: if the person is wrong, even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
item.content:encoded:
Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: if the person is wrong, even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.

Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders stuck at single-digit outbound reply rates who don't know what to change.

0:00 Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So before automating, do at least a hundred outbound attempts by hand — genuinely by hand: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

1:04 Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
Founders routinely spend hours rewriting email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — it sent hundreds of emails and of course got no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

2:06 Work backwards from closed customers to the target title
How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal through, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired over a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

3:09 List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a pile of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether it's really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, because they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, a company under 100 people probably hasn't introduced job levels yet, and one over 500 has probably already set its salary bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

4:09 Shake the tree of your personal network for your first customers
When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: your personal network first, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

5:10 Executives don't care about your product features
The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep the buyer up at night: what gets him fired, what gets him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think ‘this is exactly my problem’, they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't fully understand or trust your solution yet. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is hitting their quarterly targets. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

6:14 A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, it uses no jargon, it doesn't try to look impressive, it reads like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first line — ‘I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.’ The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works — it only talks about how to help the other person solve their problem.

8:20 On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the number one predictor
If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: having a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company that states clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite your one-line headline and your about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut what's irrelevant — if the about section is a long list of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so accumulate relevant mutual connections with your target audience — it takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

item.title: World Models Are Not Video Generation: Atlas Makes 3D Control an Input
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-a16z-世界模型不是视频生成-atlas-把-3d-控制做成了输入/
item.description: Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move is not generating longer video but putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.
item.content:encoded:
Language models process tokens; world models process physical space. Atlas's key move is not generating longer video but putting the camera and reference images into 3D coordinates as inputs, turning generation from a slot machine into directing.

23 minutes, medium information density, but Justin draws the line between world models and video generation very clearly. Worth listening for anyone working in 3D, robotics, or VFX.

1:05 Atlas is a model release, not a product release
Justin clarifies right at the start: Atlas is not a product, it is World Labs' foundation model; products come later. It does three things — generate worlds that don't exist, reconstruct from real spaces, and run simulation inside reconstructed spaces. Generation can start from text or an image, and then you can directly fly the camera through that world; reconstruction can use just one photo, or you can hand it a hundred or more, and the more photos the more accurate the reconstruction; simulation is aimed at VFX and robotics. That ordering itself shows World Labs doesn't intend to start with a consumer app, but to first stand up a horizontal foundation model and then let products grow on top of it.

4:09 Reference images are pinned into 3D space, not fed to the model
Video models tend to drift and hallucinate their own direction once generation reaches around ten seconds. Justin says Atlas's answer is spatial context: the reference images you give it are not ordinary images but are grounded in 3D space, so you can specify ‘put this one here, that one there’. When generating video you also don't just give a text prompt — you directly control the camera, telling it to fly in this direction or that, achieving precise pixel-level control. So even if you generate out to a minute, it isn't pulling a slot machine; you are generating, directing, and controlling what the model outputs.

7:10 Atlas moves the 2D/3D fork earlier
Compared with Marble, World Labs' first product, Atlas is a completely rebuilt model stack. Marble put Gaussian splat at the center: outputting video, 3D scenes, or mesh all had to pass through a Gaussian representation first, then be rendered back to images or video. Atlas breaks that dependency: the architecture is more unified and easier to scale, and the 2D/3D fork happens earlier. Generating 2D or video output is no longer bottlenecked on a Gaussian scene — the model directly produces 2D pixels; only in applications where you genuinely need 3D does it lift to 3D.

8:10 Gaussian isn't obsolete, it's just no longer mandatory
Justin doesn't think Gaussian has been outgrown; it's a tool, and you use it in the right place. VFX's final product is a 2D image or video, and may not need explicit 3D at all. But in real-time applications and on embedded devices, explicit 3D representations like Gaussian and mesh still have a place: in the future you might stream pixels in real time from a server farm, but we're not there yet, and it would be very expensive, so for client-side rendering, mobile, and VR devices, Gaussian or mesh remains useful. Another role is plugging into existing workflows — people in games, VFX, design, and architecture already have pipelines built on 3D representations, and rather than making them switch all at once to fully AI-native, it's better to let AI enter their workflows.

11:13 Simulation fills the last stretch of robot training
On the value of real to sim for robots, Justin says the first thing is evaluation: a robot ultimately has to work in a specific factory, on a specific machine, in a specific environment, and you need to make sure it works in exactly that environment. So simulation is useful in the last stretch of training and evaluation — build a simulation as close as possible to the final use case, then either fine-tune a pretrained robot foundation model directly in that simulation, or run evaluation to confirm it works. That gives you a path different from ‘collect lots of demonstrations or human teleoperation’. He also describes a more aggressive version: take a few photos or a few casual videos with your phone, reconstruct the space with Atlas, describe the task in natural language, and let an agent build the simulation and do RL fine-tuning, yielding a robot adapted to that space within minutes.

14:16 OpenAI dropping world models may be an innovator's dilemma
The host asks why OpenAI turned that Sora direction — ‘video generation models are world simulators’ — into a consumer product back then, and now isn't doing world models. Justin says he won't comment on OpenAI's internal strategy, but offers one explanation: there may be an innovator's dilemma — you're holding LLMs, which are very strong, and you're leading in that direction, so investing in the next thing isn't necessarily worthwhile. World Labs' judgment is that there is another class of models here, with a lot of opportunity, and they want to be the ones who seize it.

18:21 Three iPhones shoot bullet time, far better than expected
Asked about hard physics, Justin says he hasn't tried a black hole and guesses it wouldn't be too impressive. But what really surprised him was bullet time: three iPhones on tripods doing synchronized capture, then using Atlas to do a frozen-frame, orbit-around recomposition. He cites the official example — a strawberry dropping into oat milk, freezing time at the instant the milk splashes up, flying around it in a circle, and the effect is completely insane. This capability needs only three input viewpoints. That shows Atlas's value isn't only in ‘generating new worlds’ but also in turning a small amount of real footage into shots that traditionally required a large camera array.

19:21 3D is underrated on the input side
Justin says 3D has value in two places. On the output side people have already talked about it — sometimes you just need explicit 3D assets to drop into a workflow or game engine. But 3D's value on the input side is underrated: even if the final output is a 2D VFX shot, letting the model provide a 3D control surface helps the director decide what kind of scene the model should output. You don't want to write ‘push in, pull out, move left’ in text alone; you want to grab the camera directly and have it zoom exactly the way you want — something text simply cannot describe. So Atlas makes camera control a native input type: one of the modalities in the multimodal mix is the camera.

item.title: Making a furin site isn't hard at all — admitting it isn't rare is
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-twiv-造一个-furin-位点根本不难-难的是承认它不罕见/
item.description: Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.
item.content:encoded:
Deep sequencing shows that a few genomes in every thousand carry an insertion, and a furin site has been hit independently at the same position at least three times — the probabilistic argument for a lab origin doesn't hold up.

The first half is the quantitative methodology of viral recombination and insertion; the second half is the real target of this episode: dismantling the lab-origin argument with numbers. Listeners who want the argument can jump straight to 52 minutes.

6:07 They changed the GFP sequence and the recombination rate went up
The team first built an OC43 reverse-genetics system and made a pair of viruses: each carries a frameshifted GFP, so infection alone yields only fragments, but coinfection lets recombination stitch green fluorescent protein back together. They expected that changing the nucleotide sequence of one of the GFPs would lower the recombination rate; instead it rose. Paul says there is only a hypothesis for this, no data — one possibility is that after double-stranded RNA forms, the strand-transfer events of recombination become more likely because the duplex "breathes." This counterintuitive result later became the reagent starting point for the whole paper.

11:12 Knock GFP out of frame and let insertions reveal themselves
Measuring insertions and deletions is far harder than measuring point mutations, because they were thought to be rare and sequencing depth was insufficient. Their approach was to put the GFP gene into the viral genome and then deliberately knock it out of frame, preceded by a start-codon peptide that is in a different frame from GFP, so the virus does not glow green; it turns green only when that site acquires an insertion or deletion of a particular length that pulls GFP back into frame. This lets them count event frequencies and also pick out green viruses, read back their sequences, and infer the mechanism. This is where figure 1 of the paper comes from.

13:15 Knocking out NSP15 made insertions go down, not up
The original hypothesis came from prior work, which held that NSP15, a nuclease, affects the deletion rate — think nuclease and you naturally think deletions, not insertions. But the experiment went the opposite way: viruses with NSP15 showed a greatly increased rate of acquiring insertions that pull GFP back into frame. Paul says the deletion rate numbers were not good enough this time to quantify, but the insertion result was black and white, and they were very surprised at the time — it was this accidental result that opened up the entire line of research.

22:26 Every base sequenced a million times before you talk frequency
They moved from picking green viruses to brute-force sequencing: concentrate about 10 milliliters of virus down to 1 milliliter, load part of it onto a sequencing chip, and produce hundreds of millions of reads, so that every nucleotide in the genome is sequenced at least a million times, with roughly 30 human genomes' or 3 million viral genomes' worth of data per virus stock. Paul stresses that depth has to match the number of virions in the sample — sequencing hundreds of millions of times when there are only a thousand virions in the tube is meaningless; they calibrated to sequence roughly a few percent of the viruses in the sample.

27:32 Eleven nucleotides is the threshold for judging origin
Short insertions (three to six nucleotides) can arise randomly in a viral genome, so their origin cannot be determined, and they were excluded from the analysis. They calculated that if an 11-nucleotide stretch perfectly matches the viral genome, the probability of that being pure chance is below 5%, so they restricted the analysis to insertions of 11 nucleotides or more. The result: over 90% matched the viral genome perfectly or nearly perfectly, and in OC43 wild-type virus had 87 times more insertions than the NSP15 mutant, most of them from the positive strand.

36:41 Insertions aren't rare events — they're a few per thousand
Vincent says that for years he was told insertions are rare, but the data suggest this has been happening all along. Paul responds that "rare" is a relative term: one in a million is rare, but if you have ten million of them, it's common. The insertion frequency they give is a few genomes per thousand — roughly five to ten genomes carrying an insertion out of a thousand virions. That frequency is lower than the point-mutation rate, but not by much. The reason it seemed rare in the past is that the vast majority of insertions are harmful or even lethal to the virus and get purged at low multiplicity of infection, so you cannot isolate them.

55:05 Making a furin site isn't hard at all
Mechanistically, a furin cleavage site needs at minimum two arginines, RXXR, and can even be cleaved with a single arginine plus other amino acids in support. Six of the 64 codons encode arginine, so multiplying the two fractions, roughly 1% of random 12-base sequences can encode an RXR motif. There are about 30,000 different positions in a coronavirus genome where an insertion mutation can occur. So this is not some enormous engineering challenge.

57:08 Lightning strikes the same spot at least three times
Put the frequency of insertions, the number of insertable sites, and the size of the viral population together, and the probability of a furin cleavage site appearing at one particular position in a coronavirus genome is not astonishing — and it roughly matches what deep sequencing actually measured. In their deep-sequencing data, which did not cover the whole population, they had already found new furin cleavage sites independently at least three times at the exact position of SARS-CoV-2's existing furin site. Paul says the numbers in the paper are an underestimate: they focused PCR on just the spike region and required insertions to match the viral genome perfectly in order to rule out PCR artifacts, which very likely also excluded some naturally occurring sites that really exist.

item.title: Rome Won With a Crow: The Key to the First Punic War
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-13-ancients-罗马的胜利靠一只乌鸦-第一次布匿战争的关键/
item.description: Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.
item.content:encoded:
Rome turned sea battles into land battles with a boarding bridge called the corvus, cancelling Carthage's advantage in seamanship; but Carthage brought in a Spartan to rebuild its army and captured a Roman consul in return.

This episode tells the First Punic War as a war story with mechanisms: the crow bridge, the sacred chickens, mercenaries, war elephants — all backed by concrete images and numbers, at high information density.

2:03 This was not a war between two equal powers
The host opens by calling this a clash of ‘the two great powers of the western Mediterranean’, and Eve MacDonald corrects him on the spot: at the outbreak of the war, Carthage was not necessarily a military power of that rank. Carthage had money, controlled the sea routes, and had centuries-old networks of allies in western Sicily, but it had no strong standing army — it relied on allies and mercenaries. What actually made Carthage into a power capable of fighting Rome as an equal was this war itself. So the story Roman sources tell over and over, of ‘Roman adaptability’, is only half the story; the other half is Carthaginian resilience and adaptability, without which there is no explaining why this war lasted more than twenty years.

15:29 Mercenaries at Messana dragged both powers into war
The trigger was not the ambition of Rome or Carthage but a group of Campanian mercenaries called the Mamertines. They had seized Messana, and after being defeated by Hiero II, king of Syracuse, they split in two: one faction asked Carthage for help, the other asked Rome. Carthage acted first from its base in the Lipari Islands, and Rome came too — and not as a small intervention, but as a full invasion with two consular armies. Eve points out that the Roman sources' claim of an ‘accidental empire’ is highly suspect, because the Romans showed up at Messana at the scale of an invading force. Polybius treats the Romans' first crossing of the sea into Sicily as the starting point of Roman imperial expansion.

28:14 The corvus turned a sea battle into a land battle
Carthage was a naval power: its rowers were skilled, its ships built fast and well, and the Romans even built their own warships to Carthaginian standards. But the Romans added one thing: the corvus, meaning ‘crow’, a boarding bridge that could hook an enemy ship. Once hooked, the Carthaginian ship could not move, and Roman marines simply walked across and fought a land battle. At the Battle of Mylae the Carthaginians clearly did not expect this, and took heavy losses. Eve also cautions that the details of the corvus leave many unanswerable questions in the sources, but ancient historians all treated it as decisive. At the Battle of Cape Ecnomus the corvus was again credited as the chief factor, and Rome thereby opened the sea route for its invasion of Africa.

38:40 Carthage hired a Spartan to rebuild its army
After the Roman landing in Africa the Romans pushed forward, and it looked as though Carthage was finished. Carthage's response was to recruit a new army in the eastern Mediterranean and to bring in a Spartan commander, Xanthippus. He reorganised the Carthaginian army and reworked how the war elephants were used. Eve notes in particular that the Carthaginians had not used war elephants before; it was only after seeing the Indian elephants Pyrrhus brought that they realised they had a smaller African elephant of their own they could use. Xanthippus's reforms worked: the Roman army was destroyed and the consul Regulus was captured. This was Rome's first devastating defeat in the war, and it became a key event in later Roman memory defining the relationship between Rome and Carthage.

43:11 The captured consul went back to Rome to argue against peace
Carthage sent the captured consul Regulus back to Rome to negotiate peace. In the Senate, Regulus said not to surrender, that Carthage was there for the taking. By agreement, if peace was not made, he had to return to Carthage and remain a prisoner. He went back, and died in captivity. Eve says the various horrific versions of how he died are not actually mentioned in the credible sources, so it is hard to judge how much is later embellishment; but what is certain is that he died in captivity in Carthage, peace was refused, and Rome fought on. This passage is a classic moment of Roman self-congratulatory rhetoric.

46:27 The sacred chickens would not eat, and the Roman fleet was finished
In 249 BC, the Roman consul Tiberius Claudius Pulcher led a fleet against Carthage off Drepana. By Roman ritual, the sacred chickens on his ship had to eat for battle to be joined, otherwise it was a bad omen. The chickens would not eat, so he threw them into the sea, saying that if they would not eat, then let them drink. Roman sources present this as the most serious act of sacrilege, and the Roman fleet was then defeated at Drepana. Eve says that once Roman sources start emphasising a commander's arrogance and contempt for tradition, it usually means something bad happened. This defeat kept Rome from sending out a fleet for eight years.

50:48 Hannibal's father held Rome down with guerrilla war
After Drepana the Romans vanished from the sea, and Carthage gained freedom of action on the western coast. In 247 BC Carthage sent a new commander, Hamilcar Barca — Hannibal's father. He brought a force Polybius calls the Mix-Hellenes, made up of soldiers of Greek, Libyan and Phoenician descent from North Africa, and waged guerrilla war against Rome, occupying the high ground above Drepana and Panormus, with considerable success. Eve says this was the first time in the war that the Carthaginian army fought Rome this well. He also seized the temple complex at Eryx, sacred to the goddess the Carthaginians called Astarte, and both sides fought fiercely for this holy site.

57:20 The rams from this war still lie on the seabed
The Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC was the last battle. The Roman fleet hid behind the islands and ambushed a Carthaginian fleet heavy with supplies meant for Hamilcar. Eve says that if you go up on Eryx today, on a clear day you can see the Aegates Islands perfectly, and Hamilcar very likely watched this disaster unfold from land. Even more remarkable, the site of this sea battle was preserved underwater: over the past twenty years, underwater archaeologists have found large bronze rams on the seabed near the island of Levanzo, some inscribed with the names of Roman consuls, some bearing Punic inscriptions and carvings, along with Monte Fortino helmets and amphorae.

item.title: A Bunsen Burner Doesn't Reduce Plate Contamination, and Vegetables Protect the Heart by Another Mechanism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-thisweekinmicr-本生灯不减少平板污染-蔬菜护心另有机制/
item.description: A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.
item.content:encoded:
A Bunsen burner may actually increase settle-plate colonies in low-contamination environments; the cardiovascular benefit of vegetables may not run through the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway but through gut bacteria turning nitrate and iron into DNIC that directly activates sGC.

The first half has a clean experimental design and a counterintuitive conclusion; the second half's DNIC paper has a complete mechanism but dense terminology, suited to people willing to chew through mechanism.

6:05 A Bunsen burner does not reduce plate contamination
The authors used paired settle plates: one placed next to a lit Bunsen burner, one next to an unlit burner, both exposed simultaneously to the same contamination airflow. The lit burner overall did not lower average contamination, and the statistical comparison showed no significant improvement. This directly challenges the common claim that there is a general sterile halo around the blue flame. The authors do not say the burner never helps, but that the effect depends on environmental conditions — they deliberately contaminated the lab air with Gordonia rubripertincta, then compared different flame sizes and dry versus wet particles.

10:13 83 CFU per minute is the crossover point
Under dry-particle conditions with an average 18 mm flame, they observed an apparent crossover point: when the airborne microbial concentration was above 83 CFU/minute, settle plates next to the Bunsen burner tended to show less deposition; below that level, deposition tended to increase instead. This can explain decades of contradictory anecdotal experience: people in dry environments genuinely believe the burner helps, while people in modern air-conditioned labs with low airborne contamination genuinely find it useless or even worse. Relative humidity in a typical modern air-conditioned lab is usually between 40% and 60%.

13:43 Airflow is not one-dimensional, so don't light a burner in a laminar flow hood
The traditional view is that convection pulls contaminants upward, but the authors point out that the same airflow may first drag contaminated air laterally across the work surface before it rises. Any upward airflow must draw replacement air from somewhere, so the most important thing during aseptic work is to limit wind or airflow. This leads to the most practical point in the episode: there is no reason to light a Bunsen burner inside a laminar flow hood, since the flame itself disrupts the laminar flow. The authors did not directly visualize airflow; they measured a biologically relevant outcome — contamination — rather than fluid dynamics directly, and the authors themselves list this as a limitation.

17:49 Flaming tube mouths and lighting the burner are both ritual
The authors draw a historical comparison with the old practice of flaming culture tube mouths. Michael's graduate advisor at the time said stop doing it, there is no evidence it helps, and produced the 1972 paper proving it. The judgment in the episode is that changing behavior is hard, especially when a ritual gives a sense of control — lighting the burner feels proactive, flaming the tube mouth feels like protecting the culture, but there is no evidence it actually does anything. The authors do not argue for abandoning the Bunsen burner; they argue for measuring: use simple settle plates to measure your own lab's environment and let evidence guide practice.

28:14 Vegetables may protect the heart via the DNIC pathway
This Cell paper proposes reframing the entire nitric oxide synthase pathway: not a local paracrine model (eNOS makes NO that acts on adjacent smooth muscle), but an endocrine-like circuit — nitric oxide synthase makes nitrate, nitrate enters the gut, microbes turn it into dinitrosyl iron compounds (DNIC), which then act on targets such as the heart. If it holds up, the cardiovascular benefit of dietary nitrate (leafy greens, beets) may be mediated mainly by microbially generated DNIC, rather than the nitrate-nitrite-NO pathway we currently assume. The author is Andrei Kleshioff at the Karolinska Institute.

31:32 No DNIC can be found in germ-free mice
They used electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) to directly detect DNIC in tissue. In healthy mice, a signal is visible in liver and kidney, but when the same detection was done in germ-free mice, no DNIC at all could be found in tissue — the first hint that microbes are making it. After feeding inorganic nitrate, liver DNIC levels rose in conventional mice but not in germ-free mice; if ferric citrate was added to the nitrate drinking water, the liver DNIC signal rose even higher, while ferric citrate alone had no effect. The same in vitro: mouse and human feces plus nitrate plus iron can produce DNIC, while germ-free mouse feces cannot.

39:55 DNIC activates sGC directly, not via free NO
They used isolated mouse aortic rings, first pre-contracted with phenylephrine, then added DNIC. To distinguish free NO from direct sGC activation, they used two pharmacological tools: one that scavenges free NO, and one that directly blocks sGC. The sGC blocker completely abolished the DNIC-induced relaxation, while the free-NO scavenger only partially attenuated it. The conclusion is that DNIC activates sGC, but not through free NO — the FeNO2 entity itself appears to directly activate sGC. The same goes for bacterially generated DNIC: only wild-type E. coli supernatant (anaerobic, with nitrate and iron) relaxed aortic rings, while a mutant lacking nitrate reductase did not.

47:16 DNIC suppresses leucine uptake and holds down mTORC1
On the metabolic side, they measured the phosphorylation state of key proteins in the liver mTORC1 pathway. In disease-model mice, mTORC1 was overactivated, downstream S6K1 phosphorylation was elevated, and transcription factors driving lipid synthesis were also elevated. Both DNIC treatment and nitrate-plus-iron supplementation brought these markers back to control levels. Mechanistically, they used glioblastoma cells to measure radiolabeled leucine uptake and found that DNIC inhibits leucine uptake in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting it inhibits the leucine transporter — leucine is the key signal telling mTORC1 that nutrients are available, so blocking uptake blocks mTORC1 activation.

item.title: Private Credit's Risk Is Hidden in Insurers' Ratings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-excessreturns-私募信贷的风险藏在保险公司的评级里/
item.description: Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.
item.content:encoded:
Private credit has poured into insurance companies, much of it in affiliated investments, rated by private agencies that are systematically too generous; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400-500 billion of capital a year.

The first half is industry lore; the real value is in the middle and back sections — the specific mechanics and numbers on private credit ratings, private equity in 401ks, and Social Security reform.

5:08 A stock fund should be 80-90% stocks
When Bob Posen took over as Fidelity's president in 1995, the firm was in an awkward spot: Jeff Vinick had moved half of the Magellan fund into cash, which both dragged on performance and violated holders' expectations of a stock fund. His approach was to build internal consensus first — if the fund you run is a stock fund, you have to keep 80% to 90% of the position in the kind of stocks the fund's name implies; if you want balanced, if you want a money market fund, the firm has other products. His logic: investors bought this fund's positioning, and a manager cannot change that positioning just because he thinks "now is not a good time to buy stocks." That rule later became basic discipline for Fidelity's stock funds.

8:12 After doubling in size, keep the startup feel by splitting into small teams
Under Posen, Fidelity's assets under management grew from $500 billion to $1 trillion. His judgment was that the key to managing that much money is not process but how to preserve entrepreneurial spirit and a sense of belonging. The method was to split the investment team into a number of relatively small groups — value, growth, small cap, international — so each group had a stronger sense of ownership over results. At the same time he consolidated money market and bond funds in New Hampshire, because fixed income and money market funds look at the same credits, and here scale is a friend that spreads out enormous economies of scale; stock funds are exactly the opposite.

19:21 Put private equity in 401ks, but cap it at 10-20% first
Posen is reserved about putting private equity into 401ks. The core problem is liquidity: if a participant puts all of their retirement assets into a single private equity fund, they simply cannot get the money out when hit with a medical emergency or when they reach the age for required minimum distributions. His proposal is that private equity can only be part of an asset-allocation fund or a target-date fund, not a standalone option; if it must be a standalone option, employers should set a cap, and the magnitude he gives is 10% to 20%. He draws an analogy to employer stock: GE employees who put their whole 401k into GE stock did not end up well, and a retirement account needs diversification.

21:25 The instant markup in secondary trades is an accounting loophole
Private equity is hard to value to begin with, and what worries Posen most is secondary trades: a private fund, needing to raise cash or nearing the end of its investment period, sells part of its portfolio at a discount to another private fund. There is a technical loophole in the accounting rules that lets the buyer immediately mark that investment up to face value on the books, even if it bought at a 5% discount. He thinks that rule has to change. Valuation is already hard enough; this kind of "instant markup" should not be allowed to lift book value out of thin air and pass it through to holders via NAV.

24:28 Private ratings systematically overstate private credit
The private credit held by insurance companies can reach as much as $2 trillion on different measures, and a large share of it is "affiliated investment" — starting with Apollo, more and more private equity firms have become owners of insurance companies and then put debt related to themselves into their own insurers. Posen and his co-authors found that a great deal of private credit is rated by private rating agencies, and that rating shopping exists. Two studies, from Columbia and Imperial College, show these private ratings are systematically too high; on correct ratings, insurers would have to hold an extra $400 billion to $500 billion of capital a year. His solution is direct: make the private ratings public and let the market pick apart the assumptions and methodology.

29:35 Mark Walter's $20 billion of affiliated credit is a wake-up call
Posen treats the Mark Walter case as a wake-up call. Walter founded Guggenheim and figured out early that buying a life insurer lets you steer a formerly conservative insurance portfolio into higher-yielding securities, including private credit related to Guggenheim or to its own portfolio companies. The rules themselves allow insurers to invest in affiliated private credit, provided it is disclosed to regulators. Regulators have now found that insurers controlled by Walter or Guggenheim hold about $20 billion of affiliated private credit, some of which may have been used to buy the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Lakers. Walter's side is trying to divest part of the affiliated credit. Posen stresses this is not just Guggenheim: large private funds such as Apollo and KKR have all found insurance companies to be handy investment vehicles.

41:52 Someone with $1 million investable should not hold 40% bonds
Posen points out that most target-date funds are 80% bonds and cash, 20% stocks at retirement, which is reasonable for someone who has to live off the retirement portfolio. But more than 7 million people in the US have investable assets (excluding their primary residence) of over $1 million; they do not live off investment income and can ride out a down year in stocks. He calculates that over 30 years, a 60/40 portfolio and the 90/10 he advocates (90% stocks, 10% cash) differ by a factor of two in terminal value — the equivalent of $5 million versus $2.5 million. He rebuts the objections one by one: over the past 60 years bonds acted as a hedge in only 10 of them; in 2022 stocks and bonds both fell about 18%; stocks do fall deeply, but look at two years, five years — after 2008, 2002 and 1974 they recovered and went higher.

50:09 Semiannual reports are fine, but don't scrap first- and third-quarter filings
Posen supports keeping quarterly reporting and opposes moving to semiannual. The reason is that the economy, diplomacy and companies' own circumstances all change fast, and six months is a long time; moreover, the information vacuum created by semiannual reporting encourages insider trading. His compromise: at mid-year and year-end, file full 10-Qs and 10-Ks; in the first and third quarters, file a slimmed-down report, three or four pages plus the income statement and balance sheet — not a big burden. He rebuts the claim that "less reporting encourages long-termism": when the UK made the move from quarterly to semiannual reporting optional in 2013-14, he and a quantitative accounting scholar at Columbia compared the two groups of companies, and the companies that switched to semiannual did not invest more in R&D or capital expenditure.

item.title: For thousands of years humans fought stench, and perfume began as smoke burned for the gods
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-extracredits-人类几千年对抗恶臭-香水最初是烧给神的烟/
item.description: Perfume did not start as luxury pleasure but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they walled themselves in with scent.
item.content:encoded:
Perfume did not start as luxury pleasure but as religious incense and disease prevention — Europeans believed foul air spread disease, so they walled themselves in with scent.

Medium information density, but it strings together perfume's religious origins, the plague and the decline of bathing, and the transformation of Grasse in France into one line — suited to anyone interested in the history of the senses and the history of consumption.

0:02 Ambergris comes from a battle inside a whale
The episode opens with a very concrete image to explain where ambergris comes from: a sperm whale swallows a giant squid, the squid's hard beak lodges in the whale's intestine, gets wrapped in a mysterious bile secretion and expelled, then drifts in ocean currents for decades before washing ashore. Apothecaries buy it by gold weight, grind it into a fixative, and use it to control how fast a scent evaporates, so the fragrance shifts slowly over a whole day. The image shows how absurdly long the raw-material chain of perfume can be — behind one scent lies a deep-sea battle and decades of drifting on the currents.

2:04 Smell is the most emotional sense
The episode offers a judgment: by some measures smell is the most emotional sense, because it connects directly to the brain's memory center. Research shows that recalling a smell evokes memory more than visualizing does. Host Rob says his earliest memory is grabbing the rope seat of a lounge chair on Oahu's North Shore while learning to walk — what he remembers is not the image but the smell of that old rope fiber soaked in sea-salt air. The other host's earliest olfactory memory is the old 1980s recipe of Trix cereal. Smell can offend, can give pleasure, can summon the past like a ghost, and is essentially untouchable, changeable, and fleeting.

3:04 The earliest perfume was smoke burned for the gods
Ancient perfume's origins were mainly religious, and it was not today's distilled liquid — the earliest was basically smoke produced by burning. Egyptian priests burned specific woods, plants and resins to make pleasing smoke that both purified the ritual space and served as a channel for connecting with the gods. The word perfume comes from the Latin perfumum, meaning "through smoke." In China, Southeast Asia and Native American communities alike, these fragrances were believed to be vehicles for communicating with deities, carrying prayers and pleas up to heaven or the spirit world. In Asia this grew into an incense-making tradition that largely replaced personal perfume until modern times, because the scent stayed in clothing and rooms.

7:07 Ibn Sina invented steam distillation
In the 11th century the Arab scholar Ibn Sina discovered steam distillation: boiling a solid substance in water, collecting the steam, and separating the oil or essence from it. The first things extracted this way were rose water and rose oil, still a main ingredient in cosmetic perfumes today. Like many chemical, scientific and mathematical concepts, the method passed in the Middle Ages from Arab to European scholars, and then to Italy, which thereby became the center of European perfume-making throughout the Renaissance. The people making perfume then were often alchemists and apothecaries, and the perfumes they made were both drunk as medicine and worn on the body.

8:08 Scent was treated as an airborne barrier against disease
Before germ theory, European medical thought rested on miasma theory: foul or bad-smelling air was the main route by which disease spread. In an age without science this was not absurd, because rotting flesh, industrial burning and contaminated water really did make people sick. So Europeans concluded that inhaling sweet or pleasant air could ward off disease. The upper classes began using nosegays (a small bunch of dried flowers or herbs, held up to the nose when passing bad smells), gentleman's canes topped with a container of aromatic substances, and perfumes worn, drunk or used to fumigate clothing as protection. Most famous is the plague doctor's mask, its hooked bird beak stuffed with flowers, spices and herbs.

9:08 The Black Death killed the public bathhouse
The Black Death may be the single biggest factor in Europe's adoption of perfume. The plague that swept Europe for three centuries killed off the public baths left over from the Roman Empire, because people believed water was a vehicle of infection. Moral norms then shifted, religious concern about public nudity grew, and bathhouses came to be seen as places for trysts or sex work. People switched to cleaning their hands and faces with damp cloths, and soaking baths became increasingly rare. They began wearing more underclothes, to absorb sweat and odor so the garments could be changed and washed. In this environment, not only the upper class but the emerging middle class relied more on perfume, often making it at home from rosemary in the garden or alcohol plus purchased ingredients.

10:09 Scented gloves set off a political scandal
In the 16th century people usually scented their clothes rather than their bodies, and scented gloves, handkerchiefs and fans were especially popular. The French queen Catherine de Medici brought Italian perfumery traditions to the French court and hired the Italian perfumer Renato Bianco (Master Rene) to blend exclusive scents for her. Legend has it that Master Rene had a secret tunnel connecting his residence to Catherine's bedroom, and that he also served as her poisoner. When Catherine's rival Jeanne III of Navarre died after receiving a pair of scented gloves from Catherine, rumors spread that the gloves had been soaked in poison. Whether the poisoned gloves were real or not, several deaths were reportedly attributed to them, to the point that William Cecil advised the perfume-loving Elizabeth I to refuse any gift of scented clothing.

12:09 Grasse shifted from leather tanning to perfume
Catherine de Medici's passion for perfume changed the industry forever. The French city of Grasse realized the flower fields around it made it an ideal place for fragrance manufacturing, and with Catherine's support shifted its economic base from leather tanning to perfume-making; the city, and the country as a whole, remain the center of world perfume manufacturing to this day. France began to dominate the spice and fragrance trade, and the French empire could bring in novel, far-flung raw materials from the Caribbean, Indonesia, India and China. French perfumers also created the language we use to describe perfume, and the three stages of a fragrance's evolution: top notes or head notes smelled in the first few minutes, middle notes that can last for hours, and base notes smelled in the evening or the next day. This evolution comes from fixatives controlling evaporation speed, such as ambergris or alcohol, revealing layers of scent over time.

item.title: Astra crosses the AGI threshold, but nobody can audit it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-12-cogrev-astra-跨过-agi-门槛-但没人能审计它/
item.description: Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.
item.content:encoded:
Astra frees humans from ever doing certain tasks again, yet OpenAI paused only half its RL compute; external audit is structurally locked out until two or three days before release, and there is no adult in the room to take the blame.

The two hosts chain together the capability evidence for Astra, the true magnitude of OpenAI's pause announcement, why auditing can't get off the ground, and why doomers can't hedge by shorting — high information density.

3:30 Astra holds long tasks together with a single notes file
In the past, models handling long tasks compressed a million tokens into a summary and opened a new window, losing all the detail. Astra instead maintains a long-lived notes file that the model updates at any time and carries forward with it, no matter how many tokens have already been written, and it can also search back through its own session history. So the same million-token context window can effectively manage roughly ten times that much context within a single rollout. Nathan calls this a mechanism that is "obvious in hindsight but genuinely new."

6:19 OpenAI self-reports 3.1 agent workdays per workday
In its research-acceleration blog post, OpenAI gives its own unit of measure, the "agent workday," and reports that each human workday corresponds to 3.1 agent workdays. Nathan admits the methodology is unclear; his reading is the literal one: for every eight-hour shift a human researcher puts in, the agent runs twenty-four hours in real time. The same post also has a chart grouping by human time spent and looking at Astra's success rate, effectively a substitute for the METR curve. Nathan says the METR curve hasn't been updated in a long time — not for lack of wanting to, but because the tasks aren't big enough anymore: the model iteration cycle is now shorter than the task length that needs to be measured.

21:03 External audit is structurally locked out until two or three days
Prakash breaks down why external audit can't get off the ground: there are a hundred candidates in a model's lifecycle, and the release version is only settled in the final two or three days, so external auditors get only a few days. Bringing the audit team into the company a month early runs into a second layer of problems — audit organizations are short on people and money, depend on funding from model companies, and their staff keep flowing to model companies; and if two companies agreed not to poach from audit organizations, that would itself be an antitrust problem. He says the revolving-door problem in financial-industry regulation remains unsolved to this day.

31:12 What was announced as a pause was only half a pause
Nathan reads OpenAI's RL compute chart: what was announced was a "frontier scale RL pause," but in reality, when the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, half was paused first and the other half kept running — and that half was already enough for the Astra model to take over part of OpenAI's research infrastructure; even so it wasn't fully stopped, only half was cut. As for whether the remaining blue compute labeled "non Astra" contains a model stronger than Astra, he says he doesn't know, but "I've been disappointed before." Prakash adds: the real frontier model isn't the deployed one, nor the one being trained, but the one in the researcher's head, because those ideas become models twelve to eighteen months later.

39:05 There is no adult in the room to take the blame
Prakash's rebuttal to Jacob Coxen's line that "accepting this race and entering the endgame is an arrogant gamble launched from a private company's Slack" is: then who do you want to hand it to? Pete Hegseth's Signal group? His judgment is that there is "no adult in the room" — no external savior, the whole world is held together with duct tape, and most of the smartest, most capable people to handle this are already inside these few companies. Hand the decision to government and what you get is political legitimacy, not wisdom, and not the legitimacy needed for execution. So the starting point has to be accepting that the world is just like this.

46:03 Operation Warp Speed is the precedent for a safe harbor
Nathan proposes the government should set a hard deadline the way you do with a child: you sort it out yourselves, here's the deadline, and if you can't, I come in and play the bad guy. The accompanying move is to first take the antitrust excuse off the table. Prakash counters with Operation Warp Speed: the pharma companies specifically demanded immunity from vaccine claims, wanted a safe harbor, and actually got legislation; without that exemption, they would have been sued into bankruptcy after the pandemic. So lawyers warning that "there will be retroactive reckoning in the future" is not alarmism — even if all current decision-makers agree now, it doesn't matter, because the only thing that binds future decision-makers is law, not the verbal promises of today's people.

1:00:40 FSD's mistake is putting a human in the loop
Raffi has crashed a Tesla using FSD. His judgment is that FSD's interface design is bad, because it claims human in the loop but when it actually hands control to the user it doesn't give enough time to understand the situation and decide what to do; Waymo's design premise is that there is no human to take over, so the safety argument is completely different. He personally would be willing to drive FSD again on the highway, or at least sit behind the wheel, but would be more hesitant on local streets in Palo Alto. The same company also has two kinds of code contracts: the Firefox team allows only humans to commit, while the Mozilla AI team has an entire codebase not a single human has written a line of — people only write the spec, and the whole codebase is automatically regenerated when CI builds.

1:29:15 The takeover is already complete, nobody just admits it
The key disagreement between Prakash and Daniel: Daniel hasn't realized this has already happened. The financial market itself is the paper clipper, the means of production is the financial market, and the financial market is already fully fused with AI. Humanity took roughly a hundred years to hand complete control of the means of production to the financial market. He says don't think of AI as a chat box; it's a global information process that doesn't have to run in a single box, and doesn't even have to be silicon-based — humans together with AI agents can constitute this information process. The reason Jacob became disillusioned is that he discovered in the Slack group that there was no control at all, yet he still assumed there existed somewhere in the world a group that could actually make decisions.

item.title: Enterprises will run 80% of tokens through open models, but spend only 20% of budget

item.description: Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two.
item.content:encoded:
Open models and closed frontier models are not substitutes: the vast majority of tokens will go through open models, the hardest work stays with frontier labs, and routing and orchestration connect the two.

The Ollama CEO gives first-hand token-flow data: local and cloud model mixes are completely different, and the real constraint on enterprise procurement is security, not cost.

1:03 The driver of open models is not saving money, it is control
Jeff says cost is the biggest pain point open models can solve immediately, but the enterprise north star is ‘better control over AI and customizing it for yourself’. Cost is just the part that can be solved in the short term; only after that is solved does it become about customizing models for your own use cases. The order matters: if you treat open models only as a cost-cutting tool, you will misjudge why they are spreading so fast in the Fortune 500. AT&T has already moved 40% of its token consumption to open models, currently mainly US and European models, while also evaluating Chinese models.

4:05 Two inflection points: coding agents, then OpenClaw
Ollama's cloud per-capita token usage curve has two clear inflection points. The first came early in the year, driven by coding agents — Kimi, GLM, and MiniMax launched in succession, and for the first time open models could support a coding agent. The second came in April, brought by OpenClaw, as users expanded from developers to non-developers: finance, customer service, marketing, and sales can all throw a hard problem at an open model and let it run to completion, picking tools and fetching data along the way, consuming enormous numbers of tokens. Context windows growing from 128K to over a million was the technical precondition for this explosion.

8:08 Model launch day is a 24-hour fire drill
Ollama is a coordination channel for model vendors before launch, but Jeff says getting a model a few weeks early counts as lucky; most of the work is crammed into the final 24 hours before launch. Three things have to be done at once: inference engine support (often weeks of work, to ensure it is fast, accurate, and consistent with the reference implementation), the accompanying harness (there are now many open-source harnesses like Codex and OpenCode), and capacity from hardware and inference providers — launch day is usually the biggest growth day. He compares it to an operating system: drivers, inference layer, and application runtime all have to be glued together, a combinatorial explosion problem.

14:11 Above the token is where the new scarcity lies
Jeff cites three directions from Anthropic's platform team: knowledge (connecting company data and context to the model), coordination (a single request spawns a bunch of sub-agents, some in the cloud and some local, requiring scheduling), and execution (sandboxes and compute). His judgment: tokens are already abundant, with dozens of open model providers able to supply them; what is scarce is how to orchestrate an agent from A to B above the token. Following the path of cloud computing, developers will ultimately prefer the best independent product at each layer, rather than a packaged Heroku or Google App Engine.

17:14 Stateful things will not sink into the model layer
Asked whether the harness will be absorbed by the model, Jeff's judgment is: the core loop and hooks will sink into the model, but several categories cannot. First, the state problem — models are trained on a monthly cadence and can never catch up with the latest data, so storage is a huge independent problem space. Second, credential management and security. Open models do not come with a full set of security tools the way closed providers do, and that is crucial for enterprise adoption. This explains why the stronger the models get, the more middle layers there are.

18:15 80% of tokens go through open models, but only 20% of budget
Jeff's steady-state judgment: the vast majority of tokens inside an enterprise — his figure is 80% to 90% — will go through open models, but that does not mean 80% to 90% of budget flows to open models. The open-source community is driving costs extremely low, so perhaps only 10% to 20% of spending lands on open models. The hardest work stays with frontier labs, because the best researchers are there; the broad middle is done by combining open and closed models. He uses a law firm analogy: partners delegate work to a bunch of associates.

22:19 Local and cloud model mixes are completely different
On local models, US and Chinese models are roughly neck and neck; on cloud-hosted models, it is almost entirely Chinese models. Jeff says local is a mix of US, European, and Chinese, while cloud coding agents are dominated by Chinese models. The division of use cases is also clear: coding agents write code and tests, with many hard problems, mainly relying on large cloud models; document processing and other end-to-end low-difficulty workflows run very well locally. So it is a hybrid execution model — simple tasks run locally, with a router deciding when to go to a large model.

29:25 The Flash tier of models is the precondition for unlimited tokens
Jeff says that early in the year open models had just caught up to the intelligence frontier, less than 3 months behind the closed frontier, and the next problem to solve is extreme efficiency. The key metric for models like DeepSeek Flash is not just low cost per token, but low cost per task. These models are good enough for 80% of tasks, fast, and extremely cheap, and will become the workhorse doing the grunt work. He recalls that in the ChatGPT era nobody thought about token usage, and we will eventually return to that state, but it requires model architectures specifically trained for high token volumes. The fastest-growing segment on Ollama's cloud is precisely the DeepSeek line, driven mainly by Flash adoption.
